expect:
Top band (5-6): Thorough discussion. E.g., 3D printing does not require a mould, so setup costs are low, but each unit takes time to print and finish — suitable for small batches only. Injection moulding requires an expensive steel mould (high setup cost) but produces each unit in seconds with excellent consistency and surface finish. For 500 units, injection moulding is more cost-effective overall because the per-unit cost drops sharply once the mould is made. 3D printing would only be preferable for very small quantities or complex geometries that cannot be moulded.
Mid band (3-4): Adequate discussion with some comparison.
Lower band (1-2): Basic identification of one method with limited justification.
value:
Top band (5-6): Thorough discussion. E.g., 3D printing does not require a mould, so setup costs are low, but each unit takes time to print and finish — suitable for small batches only. Injection moulding needs a mould made from steel or aluminium (high setup cost) but produces each unit in seconds with excellent consistency and surface finish. At 500 units the decision turns on the cost of the mould: once that cost is spread across the batch, moulding is cheaper per unit, but if the mould costs more than the whole batch is worth, 3D printing wins. Credit either conclusion when the cost reasoning is clear.
Mid band (3-4): Adequate discussion with some comparison.
Lower band (1-2): Basic identification of one method with limited justification.
note: F15: moulds are not always steel, and 500 units does not settle the cost comparison
